slides.title: Don't give exclusivity away before it is earned: sign a nonexclusive OEM pilot now and make North American exclusivity conditional on certification and audited volumes

paragraphs.text: BOREAL AUTONOMY  |  BOARD OF DIRECTORS  |  APRIL 2027 DECISION
Don't give exclusivity away before it is earned: sign a nonexclusive OEM pilot now and make North American exclusivity conditional on certification and audited volumes
Decision question: should Boreal grant North American exclusivity to an OEM for its industrial robot navigation software in 2027?
Board pre-read prepared November 2026 from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data). All $ figures are undiscounted; no NPV is computed, as the board requested.

slides.title: Executive summary: reject exclusivity at signing; pilot nonexclusively and switch exclusivity on only when certification and audited volumes show it pays

paragraphs.text: Executive summary: reject exclusivity at signing; pilot nonexclusively and switch exclusivity on only when certification and audited volumes show it pays

Recommendation: Decline Option X as drafted. Sign Option N, a 12-month nonexclusive pilot at $350 per robot, and agree up front the gates under which Option M (limited exclusivity) takes effect: certification passed, two audited quarters at about 9,000 robots a year, and contract protections signed.
1  The deal is worth less than it is being presented as

The $2.0M is a recoupable advance, not extra revenue: three-year OEM cash is $8.7M, not $10.7M. After $80/robot support, $0.9M/yr engineering, the $0.45M assessment and displaced direct sales, exclusivity is worth +$2.2M to +$2.8M at plan but only −$0.04M to +$0.55M at 65% volumes.
2  The evidence the board requires for irreversible exclusivity does not exist yet

Lab uptime is 98.8% against a 99.5% production bar. The third-party assessment has not started. OEM volumes are unaudited, and the 14,000 'booked devices' are a forecast. The growth claim rests on correlation. The draft lacks audit rights, a royalty floor, release triggers and code escrow.
3  The phased N→M structure beats every alternative

It earns $50 more per robot, keeps the direct channel (~$1.48M of gross margin on new ARR in 2028), and matches X's value even if the OEM ships 24–32% fewer robots. It holds cash at least $0.55M above the $2.6M buffer in the worst case, and it fails none of the board's conditions.
4  Gates, signposts and next steps make the decision reversible

Start the $0.45M assessment now; it is on the critical path for every OEM route. Convert to exclusivity only after certification and audited shipments of at least 2,250 robots a quarter. If the OEM insists on exclusivity at signing, walk away and fall back to direct sales plus the integration-firm pilot.
Source: Board briefing pack §1–7; team analysis (calculations on slides 4–7, 12–13 and appendix)

slides.title: Of six conditions that would have to hold for exclusivity at signing to be right, only one partly holds, so the 'don't sign yet' hypothesis stands

paragraphs.text: Of six conditions that would have to hold for exclusivity at signing to be right, only one partly holds, so the 'don't sign yet' hypothesis stands

Initial hypothesis (stated before testing): Boreal should not grant exclusivity at signing; a nonexclusive or milestone deal captures the OEM upside without giving up the direct channel. Test: state what must hold for the opposite answer (Option X) to be right, then check each condition against the pack.

data: For exclusivity at signing to be right, it must be true that…
1. The $2.0M signing payment adds value on top of royalties
It is an advance credited against the first $2.0M of royalties, and the partner can demand an offset. 3-yr cash is $8.7M either way (slide 4)
2. Exclusivity creates value even in the low case and with realistic channel overlap
+$2.2–2.8M at plan; −$0.04M to +$0.55M at 65% volumes with Sales' 30–70% overlap (slides 5–7)
3. The product is production-ready in the OEM's hardware
98.8% lab uptime vs 99.5% required; no loaded-warehouse or collision-heavy test; assessment not started (slide 8)
4. OEM volumes and the growth story are reliable enough to commit on
Shipments unaudited; '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders; competitor evidence is correlational (slide 9)
5. Exclusivity is the only way to win the OEM's volume
The OEM will consider Option N (nonexclusive, $350/robot) and Option M (gated exclusivity) (slides 11–12)
6. The contract protects Boreal if forecasts or certification miss
No audit right, no royalty floor after the advance, no release triggers, no code escrow (slide 10)

paragraphs.text: Result: the hypothesis survives, refined. The problem is exclusivity before evidence, not exclusivity itself, so the answer is a gated path to exclusivity rather than a flat 'no'.
Source: Board briefing pack §1–6; team analysis

How the board should describe it
Revenue = royalties earned as qualifying robots ship and payment is collected: $1.5M in 2027 at plan, not $3.5M.
The $2.0M is a minimum-guarantee liability until it is earned. The partner can demand an offset if guaranteed performance is missed.
The 'revenue win plus recurring royalties' framing double-counts $2.0M, overstating 3-year OEM income by 23% ($10.7M vs $8.7M).
What the advance buys: timing only. It brings $1.5–2.0M of cash forward into 2027, which Boreal does not need to stay above its buffer (slide 13).

Reading the table: the advance is cash received early, then netted out of 2028 royalty cash. Total cash therefore always equals royalties earned. In the stress case, 2028 royalty cash falls to $0.93M because $1.03M of credit is still being recouped.

How to read it
Grey bars show the annual OEM shipments needed for exclusivity to beat staying nonexclusive. Each robot contributes $220, which must cover $0.9M of engineering plus the displaced direct margin.
At Sales' 30–70% overlap, the hurdle is 6,100–8,800 robots a year. The plan (10,000) clears it; the stress case (6,500) clears only the 30% end.
Option M's proposed gate of 5,000 annualised is below every realistic breakeven. It should rise to about 9,000 (2,250 per quarter) unless the scope excludes customers on other OEMs' robots.
Under Option N, the OEM programme alone breaks even at 3,333 robots ($0.9M ÷ $270), and the direct channel is untouched.
Source: Board briefing pack §3–4; team analysis. Breakeven = ($0.9M + overlap × $1.476M) ÷ ($300 − $80).

slides.title: The upside case rests on unaudited volumes, an untested 'fully incremental' claim and a correlational competitor analogy

paragraphs.text: 1  VALUE
2  EVIDENCE

The upside case rests on unaudited volumes, an untested 'fully incremental' claim and a correlational competitor analogy
OEM volumes are a forecast, not a commitment
Channel overlap is unknown, and it drives the answer
'Exclusivity caused competitors' growth' is not shown
•  Quarterly shipment data are not independently audited, and the draft contract has no audit right.
•  The '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders. Treat them as a 2029 forecast.
•  The 2027 forecast of 5,000 assumes production shipments in a year when certification lands in September at the earliest.
•  The board is unwilling to rely solely on verbal OEM launch forecasts.
•  The CEO says the OEM channel is 0% overlap (entirely incremental). Sales says 30–70% of OEM buyers overlap with its pipeline.
•  Neither view is backed by customer-level identifiers.
•  Each 10 points of overlap is worth ~$0.15M a year of displaced direct gross margin ($1.8M × 82% × 10%).
•  The overlap can be measured during a nonexclusive pilot. It cannot be measured after exclusivity has closed the direct channel.
•  Five competitors' exclusive OEM deals coincided with faster growth. That is a correlation.
•  Those firms had more marketing support, more mature products and higher market share before they signed, so any of these could explain the growth.
•  Boreal has none of these advantages yet: its product is uncertified and its leverage limited.
•  No causal evidence is available, so we give this argument zero weight in the economics.

slides.title: Appendix B: formulas, data sources and the gaps the pilot should close

paragraphs.text: Appendix B: formulas, data sources and the gaps the pilot should close
Formulas used
Royalty cash (X) = royalties earned − advance credit still unrecouped (first $2.0M of royalties)
OEM contribution = robots × (royalty − $80) − $0.9M engineering per year
Exclusivity value = Σ contribution − $0.45M assessment − overlap × $1.8M × 82%
Breakeven robots/yr = ($0.9M + overlap × $1.476M) ÷ ($300 − $80)
N parity volume = (X value + $2.7M + $0.45M) ÷ ($350 − $80)
Headroom = $4.9M − $2.6M + deal cash flows to end-2027
Data gaps and how we handled them
Channel overlap: no customer-level data. We used Sales' 30–70% range, bounded by 0% and 100%.
Direct churn and later cohorts: not in the pack. The base case counts the 2028 cohort only; a 2029 renewal sensitivity is on slide 6.
Discount rate: not in the pack. No NPV is computed, per the board.
OEM enforcement terms and termination payment: not in the pack. Treated qualitatively.
Integration-firm royalty: not in the pack. Treated as a nonexclusive complement, not valued.
Rest-of-business cash burn: not in the pack. We assume the $2.6M buffer covers it.
Pricing under N/M: the OEM will not guarantee it. Shown as indicative.
